Investigation · November 20, 2026 · Updated November 23, 2026

Why did Columbus declare an emergency to lease Flock cameras?

Residents who first learned about the Flock lease from Friday afternoon’s final agenda had only until 3 p.m. Monday to sign up to speak. That left just under 72 hours, mostly over a weekend, to read the proposal and talk with neighbors about where Columbus wanted to put 38 fixed license plate readers and why it wanted to skip competitive bidding.

On Monday evening, December 9, 2024, Columbus City Council waived competitive bidding and authorized up to $228,000 for a two-year lease. Council said the cameras would help reduce violent crime and solve cases in areas already covered by ShotSpotter gunfire detectors. Police said a delay getting the purchase approved had left too little time to seek bids before a December grant deadline. By Thursday, the city had recorded an order for the full amount.

Read the lease ordinance, §§ 5–6 Watch the vote at 3:15:05 Trace the purchase order See the five pending records requests

What would another week have given residents?

The clerk last published the final agenda at 3:18 p.m. on Friday, December 6. On page 36, item SR-37 named Flock, gave the price and asked Council to waive bidding and declare an emergency. The lease had appeared on neither the November 18 nor the November 25 regular agenda. An earlier version of the December 9 agenda may have reached residents sooner. We asked the clerk for the first posting that named the lease.

Flock on the December 9 agenda, p. 36 Clerk’s final agenda timestamp November 18 agenda November 25 agenda

We checked the clerk’s timestamps for Council’s 31 other Monday evening meetings in 2024. The median time from the last agenda posting to the speaker deadline was also about 72 hours. The extra week residents ordinarily have comes between readings. The charter calls for two readings at regular meetings at least a week apart unless Council waives the rule. An emergency measure can pass at one meeting.

Clerk’s 2024 Council agenda timestamps City charter § 20, ordinary readings and exceptions

On page 7 of that same agenda was a proposal for lighting, court and path improvements at Lincoln Park. Council gave it a first reading on December 9 and approved it on December 16. Residents who saw both proposals that Friday had nearly 10 days from the posting to the speaker deadline for the park vote. Someone watching the first reading could still ask for the park plans, talk them over with neighbors and sign up to speak before the final vote. When the city explained the Flock waiver on the evening of December 9, the deadline to sign up and respond had already passed.

Lincoln Park on the December 9 agenda, FR-29, p. 7 Lincoln Park’s December 9 reading and December 16 vote

For either meeting, the online speaker form opened at 12:01 a.m. and closed at 3 p.m. on meeting day. Council allowed three speakers for an item and three against, in signup order, with three minutes each. Residents could also submit written testimony.

Clerk’s speaker signup hours Speaking rules, § 111.12

Council spent roughly 90 seconds on the lease. Councilmember Emmanuel Remy asked a Public Safety deputy director to explain the bidding waiver. The deputy director cited the December deadline and said Flock’s equipment worked with other Central Ohio systems. No resident spoke during the item. Council took a separate vote and approved the lease 8–0, with one member absent.

Hear Remy ask about the waiver at 3:15:58 Minutes and roll call, pp. 50–51

Which deadline did the city have to meet?

Flock dated its quote October 23, 47 days before the vote. It covered 38 readers and expired on December 31. Council met again on December 16, well within the dates on that quote. Police said the December deadline came from the state grant. Their written waiver also reported a $212,800 quote from Insight for cameras alone. Flock’s price included installation and a two-year lease.

Flock’s dated quote, pp. 1–3 Police waiver and Insight’s price, items 2–4

The city’s legislative system dates the waiver to November 13, 2024, 26 days before the vote. By then, police had already put the approval delay in writing. The public action history starts with Council’s vote. Residents trying to understand where those weeks went still need the internal record of who had the purchase request, when it reached them and whether anyone sent it back for changes.

City attachment log with the waiver timestamp City’s action history for the lease

Ohio signed the $228,000 award on September 5, 2024. The cover sheet gave Columbus from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2026 to complete the project and until August 29, 2026 to close it out. In October, Council authorized the city to accept the grant and budgeted the money for contractual services. That ordinance described 32 fixed readers and wiring. The December lease covered 38.

Signed state award, p. 1 October grant ordinance, budget and attachments

Ohio’s budget guide told grantees to put leased equipment under contracts, as Columbus did. Even if the cameras counted as an equipment purchase, Ohio’s published handbook gave grantees six months to commit the money, starting from the later of the project start or award date. Six months from September 5 points to early March 2025.

Ohio’s 2022 guide to budgeting a lease, PDF p. 5 Ohio’s grant handbook, archived in 2023, printed p. 14

Would waiting one more week have put the grant at risk? The public grant file leaves the deadline for ordering these cameras unresolved. The signed award refers to special conditions and an approved application. Those documents, or a separate instruction from Ohio, could establish a December ordering deadline. We asked the state for them so residents can check the explanation Council heard before it voted.

How much public money can residents trace?

The mayor signed the ordinance on December 10. An ordinary ordinance generally takes effect 30 days after passage. The emergency clause let Columbus act immediately. On December 12, before the next Council meeting, the City Auditor recorded purchase order PO483191 for $228,000.

City charter § 22, effective dates 2024 purchase orders (CSV)

Under the charter, even a properly filed referendum petition leaves an emergency ordinance in effect while residents wait for a vote. If voters later repeal the measure, the city can still pay expenses it incurred before that vote.

Columbus charter, § 44-2, p. 8

Of the $228,000 on the order, we could trace one $114,000 payment from Flock’s invoice to the bank. On May 1, 2026, the invoice journal lists INV-88264 against that purchase order. The vendor ledger records a $114,000 payment to Flock the same day. The bank register shows that payment voucher APPY141972452 cleared on May 8.

Auditor’s data catalog 2026 invoices (CSV) 2026 vendor payments (CSV) 2026 bank register (CSV)

Did anyone try to speak and miss their chance?

Anyone watching the recording can hear officials explain the waiver. What the recording leaves open is whether a resident sent a written objection, submitted a speaker slip too late or tried unsuccessfully to speak. Whether anyone intended to discourage scrutiny also remains unknown.

The clerk keeps a Speaker Slip Database for regular Council meetings. In 2025 the city’s Records Commission identified the database and emailed slips under record series CLRK-7. We asked for the SR-37 entries, written testimony and any record of late or declined signups. Those records could show who asked to speak and what written objections, if any, Council had in hand when it voted.

Records Commission minutes on speaker slips, p. 36

What records are we still waiting for?

On November 21, 2026, we filed five requests under the Ohio Public Records Act. All four Columbus offices confirmed receipt. As of November 23, 2026, we are waiting for documents from all five offices.

Ohio Office of Criminal Justice Services
Did the state give Columbus a December deadline for this lease? We asked for the full award, its special conditions and any instruction that set or changed the deadline. In a November 23, 2026 email about grant 2024-ST-VCR-V391, an Ohio Department of Public Safety records officer copied the department’s public-records office on our request. The reply gave no date for releasing the records.
Columbus Division of Police
Police cited a delay in the bid waiver. We asked for the original purchase request, the vendor quotes and the messages that explain which approval police were waiting for.
Columbus Purchasing Request 26-1691
When did Purchasing first see the request? The requisition history should show who received it, whether anyone sent it back for corrections and when it moved on.
Columbus City Auditor Request 26-1692
The ledger dates the order to December 12. We asked for the fiscal approval behind it and the record showing when the city sent the order to Flock.
Columbus City Clerk Request 26-1693
Did anyone object in writing or try to speak? We requested speaker slips for SR-37, written testimony, records of late or declined signups, and the first agenda that gave residents notice of the vote.
